opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few reasons, and some of them are quite selfish in a good way, and some of them are more about the health of the field as a whole.

The first thing is that a network protocol is only really valuable if the hardware supports it well. MRC (the multipath reliable connection work) is really about how you move data across these enormous training clusters when you've got many paths through the network and you want to use all of them at once without getting tripped up by congestion or failures. To do that efficiently, a lot of it has to live in the NICs, and potentially the switches need to cooperate in certain ways. We don't build NICs. We don't build switches. So if this stays as something only OpenAI does, we're asking vendors to build special hardware for one customer, and that's never going to get you the best silicon or the best price, and it's certainly not going to get you a mature, well-debugged implementation.

If, on the other hand, it's something the whole industry adopts, then every vendor has an incentive to make their implementation really good, there's competition, there's interoperability testing, and you get a much richer ecosystem. We benefit enormously from that.

The second reason is just that I come from the internet world, from the IETF and the academic networking community, and the lesson there over decades is that open protocols win. TCP/IP won not because it was the cleverest design at every point, but because anybody could implement it and build on it. Proprietary networking stacks tend to become dead ends. I'd much rather MRC be something people pick apart, critique, and improve, because honestly other people are going to find problems we didn't think of, and they'll find better ways to do things.

And third, there's a broader point. Training these frontier models is a networking problem as much as a compute problem now. The scale is such that the network really determines how well you can use all that very expensive hardware. If the whole industry is stuck with protocols that weren't designed for this, that's a lot of wasted capacity, wasted energy, wasted money everywhere. Raising the baseline for everyone seems like the right thing to do, and it doesn't really cost us anything competitively, because the network isn't where we want to differentiate. We want to differentiate on the models. The plumbing should just work, and it should work for everybody.

r001.rationale: The response says open protocols such as TCP/IP win, but does not attribute Ethernet’s continued use to being an open standard.

r002.rationale: It argues that broad industry adoption would bring better hardware, competition, interoperability, and improvement than keeping MRC exclusive to OpenAI.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the answer is that a transport protocol that only one company runs isn't really a transport protocol — it's a private optimization. The whole value of something like MRC comes from both ends of a connection speaking it, and the ends aren't all ours. Our traffic crosses other people's networks, lands on devices we don't control, and talks to services we don't run. If MRC stays exclusive, we get maybe a third of the benefit and we carry all of the maintenance burden forever.

There's also a history lesson here that I take pretty seriously. I spent a lot of years working on Internet protocols, and the ones that won — TCP, HTTP, more recently QUIC — won because people outside the originating organization could pick them up, poke holes in them, implement them independently, and argue about them in public. That process makes a protocol better. It finds the corner cases you didn't think of. Google could have kept QUIC in-house; the decision to take it to the IETF is a big part of why it's now deployed across most of the web, and why the final design is substantially stronger than the first version.

And frankly, the problems MRC is trying to solve aren't unique to us. Anyone streaming model outputs, doing real-time voice, running agents that are chatty back and forth with a server — they're all hitting the same latency and loss-recovery issues on the same imperfect networks. If we solve it alone, everybody else reinvents it slightly differently, and you end up with a mess of incompatible things that each work a bit worse. If it's open, middleboxes and CDNs and operating systems eventually treat it as a first-class citizen, and that's where the real gains show up.

So it's partly principle and partly self-interest, and I'm comfortable saying both. The Internet is better when the good ideas are shared, and we're better off when the protocol we depend on is something the whole ecosystem has a stake in keeping healthy.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Ethernet or attribute its continued use to being an open standard.

r002.rationale: It argues that MRC should be open and widely adopted because it benefits from independent implementation, shared improvements, and ecosystem-wide deployment, whereas keeping it exclusive limits its benefits.

And widespread adoption gives everyone a reason to support it, improve it, and build things that work with it. You get a much stronger ecosystem than you would if it remained something only OpenAI used.
